title: Report on Studying Abroad at Johns Hopkins University
paragraphs: I am 王正, who was allowed to study abroad at Johns Hopkins University from March to July 2013. What first made me interested in studying abroad was reading the experience reports of seniors on the International Exchange Office page in the second half of my fourth year, and vaguely thinking that studying abroad looked fun and that studying in America, though I did not really know what it was, seemed cool. Around that time I also learned that the common language of medicine is English, that English ability is important when considering one's ability as a doctor, and I felt a sense of crisis about my English, which had kept declining since the entrance exams. A clinical study abroad that killed two birds with one stone, improving English and experiencing American medical education, was truly attractive to me at the time.

The reasons I chose Johns Hopkins as my destination were that it is a world-class hospital, that exchange students come from all over the world so one can meet various people, and that it is used to accepting exchange students. At Johns Hopkins University, I was looked after in Anesthesia, Emergency Medicine and Hospitalist for 4 weeks, 4 weeks and 6 weeks respectively. For the first two weeks I struggled especially with the language, but as I got used to the hospital and the mechanisms of each department, I felt I gradually got the knack of the clerkship. Even so, the language barrier was big, and in particular the conversations among doctors were fast and full of abbreviations, so I struggled to understand them to the end.

1. Anesthesia I was allowed to rotate for one week each through general anesthesia, cardiac anesthesia, obstetric anesthesia, and pediatric & transplant anesthesia. Basically I attended a resident or senior doctor and did preoperative evaluation (Mallampati classification and so on), securing lines, bag-and-mask ventilation and tracheal intubation. During surgery I talked freely with the doctors about a wide range of things, from medicine to small talk. Once a week there was a Morning Round at 6 a.m., and to prepare for it, students had to go to the ward after 5 a.m. and copy vital signs and so on into the charts. During rounds, all I could do was collect the charts of the team's patients, put them on a cart and go ahead of the rounds, but as they gradually got a sense of me, their trust grew, and they even let me make the admission summaries of newly admitted patients by myself. Also, through the kindness of a doctor in obstetric anesthesia, I was allowed to go for a week to MGH and BWH in Boston.

2. Emergency Medicine Because the emergency department was on a shift system, on the first day we students consulted with the other students and made our own shifts so that they would not overlap, and we practised suturing using pig's feet. Shifts were basically of two kinds, 8 hours and 12 hours, plus the ambulance shift called EMS, and those who wished could also ride the doctor helicopter. In addition, on Friday mornings there were lectures hosted by residents for residents, attendings and students, and talks by lecturers from other universities. Incidentally, there were three kinds of 8-hour shifts, 7 a.m.-3 p.m., 3 p.m.-11 p.m. and 11 p.m.-7 a.m., but the daytime was busier, and the evening to midnight period was characterised by many trauma and GSW cases. What students did during a shift was to examine a patient, present to the resident or attending including the assessment & plan, and get feedback. After that, I helped the residents as appropriate, placing orders for that patient and following up test results. Also, despite the busyness, there were many educational doctors, and attendings frequently asked residents questions such as "What complications should we watch out for?" and "What treatments are said to be good these days?", and residents asked students "What differential diagnosis must you not forget?" and "Which antibiotic would you prescribe?", frequently doing training to sharpen one's thinking. The lecture held every Friday morning was also attended by everyone from students to attendings, and even among the doctors themselves there was frequent effort to organise memory and update information. On the last day of the clerkship, every student gave a presentation, one by one, on an impressive case encountered during the clerkship.

3. Hospitalist This is a department not yet seen much in Japan, something like a general internal medicine department specialising in inpatients. Unlike other departments there were no residents, so students had many patients to take care of, 3 to 5. When a newly admitted patient came, the basic routine was being told "Then go take the history and physical findings," making the admission summary, making my own assessment & plan and provisional test orders, and then presenting to the attending. Because there were many consults to other departments, I was allowed to do and take part in a wide range of things, from chores such as contacting other departments using a pager, calling private clinics to arrange transfers and contacting rehabilitation facilities after discharge, to mini-lectures and journal clubs. Seeing that two cases of VRE were detected among only my own patients in six weeks, I felt that Japanese hospitals have higher hygiene awareness. However, awareness of preventing needlestick injuries was very high, all needle devices had features to prevent recapping, and sharps containers were placed all over each room and corridor. Gloves during surgery were also always doubled.

Finally, during my study abroad I was helped by many people, treated to meals and kindly looked after. I would like to thank Dr. 粕谷, who made such efforts for the study abroad, and Dr. 岩間 and Dr. 林, who looked after me there. Thank you very much indeed.
